CausalChain: Chronic liver insult/iron overload -> Upregulation of NCOA4-mediated ferritinophagy -> Increased labile iron pool -> Fenton reaction and ROS generation -> Enhanced lipid peroxidation -> Depletion of glutathione due to impaired transsulfuration pathway -> GPX4 inactivation -> Hepatocyte ferroptosis -> Release of pro-inflammatory/fibrogenic signals -> Activation of hepatic stellate cells -> Exacerbation of liver fibrosis
Hypothesis: In chronic liver diseases, a synergistic interplay between heightened ferritinophagy (via NCOA4) and an impaired transsulfuration pathway leads to excessive ferroptosis in hepatocytes, which in turn promotes hepatic stellate cell activation and accelerates liver fibrosis. Targeting these pathways may provide novel therapeutic strategies to prevent progression of liver disease.
Abstract: Recent evidence underscores the crucial role of ferroptosis in the pathogenesis of liver diseases. Here, we propose that in chronic liver pathologies, such as non‐alcoholic steatohepatitis and iron overload syndrome, an imbalance between iron storage processes and cysteine replenishment via the transsulfuration pathway potentiates ferroptotic cell death in hepatocytes. Specifically, enhanced NCOA4‐mediated ferritinophagy elevates the intracellular labile iron pool, driving ROS generation and lipid peroxidation. Concurrently, an impaired transsulfuration pathway leads to insufficient cysteine, precipitating reduced glutathione synthesis and GPX4 inactivation. This dual hit not only induces hepatocyte ferroptosis but may also trigger the paracrine activation of hepatic stellate cells, thus promoting fibrosis. Our hypothesis offers a testable framework for targeting metabolic and autophagic pathways to mitigate liver fibrosis and other sequelae of ferroptotic injury.
